title: Avoiding Dilution: Using Diffusion and Vision Transformers to resolve Majorana Features in Nanowires at High Temperature
authors: Jacob R. Taylor, Haining Pan, Jay D. Sau, Sankar Das Sarma
abstract: Identifying Majorana zero modes in semiconductor--superconductor nanowires requires ultra-low temperature transport measurements in dilution refrigerators, making device screening slow and resource-intensive. Here, we investigate whether high-temperature conductance data can be used to infer low-temperature Majorana nanowire properties before committing devices to dilution-refrigerator characterization. We generate paired high- and low-temperature conductance simulations for disordered Majorana nanowires and train neural networks to perform two related tasks. First, we use a Shifted Window U-Net Transformer diffusion-inspired architecture to reconstruct low-temperature conductance from thermally broadened high-temperature measurements, achieving high-fidelity recovery with $R^2 \approx {0.95}$ for local conductance and $R^2 \approx {0.91}$ for nonlocal conductance. Second, we train a Video Vision Transformer-based network to predict the low-temperature topological visibility directly from high-temperature conductance, obtaining $R^2 \approx {0.80}$. These results demonstrate that machine-learning models can recover and infer low-temperature Majorana features from experimentally easier high-temperature data, providing a practical route for rejecting poor devices early thus avoiding slow and resource-intensive dilution refrigeration for non-promising devices. This high-temperature screening approach could substantially accelerate the experimental feedback loop for Majorana nanowire device development.
summary: This work introduces a machine-learning pipeline to overcome the experimental bottleneck of measuring Majorana zero modes at ultra-low temperatures. By training neural networks on simulated paired high- and low-temperature conductance data, the authors demonstrate that key topological features can be reliably inferred from simpler, higher-temperature measurements. This offers a practical acceleration tool for quantum device development.
main_problem: Characterizing Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in nanowires typically requires slow, resource-intensive ultra-low temperature measurements.
main_result: Machine learning models can successfully reconstruct low-temperature conductance and predict topological visibility using only easier-to-measure high-temperature data.
method: The authors employed two machine learning approaches: a diffusion-inspired U-Net Transformer for conductance reconstruction, and a Video Vision Transformer (ViViT) for direct prediction of topological visibility.
model_or_system: The study models semiconductor–superconductor hybrid nanowires hosting topological superconductors, governed by a Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian. The analysis compares high-temperature simulations to target low-temperature MZM properties.
key_observables: Local and nonlocal conductances ($G_{ii}, G_{ij}$), and the Topological Visibility (TV).
important_parameters: Ultra-low temperatures ($\approx 50 	ext{ mK}$), high-temperature measurements, disorder strength, superconducting gap $\Delta_0$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that ML models can learn the underlying physics to invert the thermal broadening effect inherent in high-temperature measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate network architectures (SWIN-Block, UNETR upsampling) and compare reconstruction/prediction results against direct measurement or inverse convolution methods.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the difficulty of low-T MZM detection. It then details using ML on paired high/low-T simulations to train two networks: one for conductance reconstruction (diffusion model) and one for TV prediction (ViViT). Results demonstrate high fidelity in both tasks.
why_interesting: The application of advanced deep learning architectures like diffusion models and Vision Transformers to extract fundamental quantum signatures from noisy, experimentally accessible data is highly relevant for open quantum systems characterization.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

The disorder levels are σdis = (a) 0.716 meV, (b) 3.55 meV, (c) 0.237 meV, and (d) 1.586 meV, with correlation lengths of (a) 27 nm, (b) 31.9 nm, (c) 47 nm, and (d) 48 nm respectively.

FIG. 5: Schematic of the SWIN-Block used in the Conductance U-Net. The block alternates standard and shifted-window attention: features are partitioned into W × W windows, processed by a window-wise transformer with H heads, stitched back together, and repeated for depth D. The shifted-window stage enables information exchange between neighboring windows.
